fix.shows: Rajeev Kumar, a former professor of computer science at IIT Kharagpur, IIT Kanpur, BITS Pilani and JNU, argues that a roll of nearly a billion electors needs a computerised database and that the trouble with the revision lies in poor governance of the exercise. He sets out six weaknesses as he sees them. The rolls of 2002 to 2004, prepared largely on paper and digitised later, are used to map electors without being checked first. The rules for logical discrepancies are not public and reportedly grew from six categories to eleven. Reports allege bulk deletions with no identifiable applicant and inserted code that generated Form 7 objections, which he says need an independent inquiry. Reports of restricted access suggest registration officers could not verify, correct or restore records. He says a pilot should have tested the mapping, the rules and the forms before the exercise began, and the Commission declined in reply to an RTI request to describe the software that flags errors. He asks for a separate form or workflow to restore wrongly deleted names in place of Form 6, and for an independent technical audit of ECINet by industry experts, possibly led by Nandan Nilekani, and he says the academic review proposed in the Commission's press note of 26 September may not be enough.
